title: Blood Relations
summary: Relationship vocabulary across generations and in-laws, a symbol diagram that keeps the family straight, and set routines for pointing-to-a-photo statements and coded-relation expressions.
learningObjectives: Name relations precisely across two or three generations, including in-laws.
Draw a family as a levelled diagram with fixed symbols.
Unpack a pointing-to-a-photo statement from the far end back to the speaker.
Evaluate a coded-relation expression one link at a time.

blocks.title: The relationship map
blocks.markdown:
Blood-relation questions sit on a small family tree with three or four generations: grandparents, parents, the people in the puzzle, and sometimes their children.

Every question is really asking you to follow a path along that tree. The work is to build the tree correctly from the wording; once it is drawn, the answer is a short walk from one person to another. Nothing depends on names or ages unless the puzzle states them.
searchKeywords: blood relations small family tree three or four generations
follow a path along the tree
build the tree from the wording

blocks.title: Relationship vocabulary
blocks.markdown:
- **Paternal** means on the father's side, **maternal** on the mother's side. Your father's brother is your paternal uncle; your mother's brother is your maternal uncle.
- **In-laws** come through marriage: your spouse's brother and your sister's husband are both your brother-in-law; your son's wife is your daughter-in-law.
- **Nephew and niece** are your sibling's children. Your **cousin** is your uncle's or aunt's child.
- **Sibling** covers brother or sister without stating which. **Spouse** covers husband or wife.
- Two people are of the **same generation** if the same number of parent-steps separates each from a shared ancestor.

blocks.title: Draw a family diagram
blocks.markdown:
Use one fixed set of marks so the picture never lies:

- A triangle for a male, a circle for a female, a plain box when the sex is unknown.
- A double line between two people who are married.
- A vertical line dropping to their children, with siblings side by side on one level.
- Keep every person of one generation on the same horizontal level, parents above, children below.

```
     A --=-- B          double line = married
         |
    +----+----+         vertical line = children
    C         D          C and D on one level = siblings
```

Add each fact to the diagram as you read it, and never carry a half-formed picture in your head.
searchKeywords: family diagram triangle male circle female box unknown
double line married vertical line children
one generation per horizontal level

blocks.title: Pointing-to-a-photo statements
blocks.markdown:
A speaker points at someone and describes them through a chain like "the only son of my grandfather's daughter". Work the chain from the **far end back to the speaker**:

1. Start at the last noun ("my grandfather") and move outward one link at a time.
2. Replace every "my" and "I" with the speaker once the chain is built.
3. Use words like "only" — "the only daughter of X" tells you X has no other daughters, which often pins the person down.
4. Read the relationship of that person to the speaker off the finished diagram.
searchKeywords: pointing to a photo statement work from the far end back
replace my and i with the speaker
only daughter of x means no other daughters

blocks.title: Coded relations
blocks.markdown:
Here each symbol fixes one relationship, and you are handed an expression to evaluate. A common key is:

- `A + B` means A is the father of B.
- `A - B` means A is the mother of B.
- `A * B` means A is the brother of B.
- `A / B` means A is the sister of B.

Build the expression left to right, one link at a time, drawing each into the diagram. The final question — say, how `A` relates to the last person — is then read straight off the picture. The sex of the end person is often not needed for the answer.
searchKeywords: coded relations symbol fixes one relationship
plus father minus mother star brother slash sister
build expression left to right read the diagram

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.markdown:
**1. Pointing.** Pointing at a boy, Meera says, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother's father." How is the boy related to Meera?

Start at the far end: "my mother's father" is Meera's maternal grandfather. "The only daughter of" him — since he has just one daughter, and Meera's mother is a daughter of his — is Meera's mother. So the boy's mother is Meera's mother, which makes the boy **Meera's brother**.

**2. Coded.** With `+` for father, `-` for mother, `*` for brother, evaluate `P + Q - R * S` and state how P relates to S.

`P + Q`: P is Q's father. `Q - R`: Q is R's mother. `R * S`: R is S's brother, so R and S share the parent Q. Q is the mother of S, and P is the father of Q. P is therefore the father of S's mother, that is, **S's maternal grandfather**.

coded relation P plus Q minus R star S maternal grandfather

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.markdown:
- **Assuming a sex** the puzzle never gave — reading "child" as "son", or "cousin" as male.
- **Confusing an uncle with a brother-in-law**, or a paternal uncle with a maternal one, when the side is stated.
- **Working a pointing statement front to back**, which tangles the "my" references.
- **Ignoring "only"** — "the only son" is often the fact that makes the answer unique.
- **Mixing levels in the diagram**, so a cousin ends up drawn as a sibling.
- **Answering with a sex** the question did not ask for, such as "grandson" when "grandchild" is all that follows.
searchKeywords: blood relations mistakes assuming sex uncle vs brother in law
pointing statement front to back tangle
ignoring only mixing diagram levels

blocks.title: Practice
blocks.markdown:
Key for the coded items: `+` father, `-` mother, `*` brother, `/` sister. Give the answer and a one-line reason.

1. `A - B + C`: how is A related to C?
2. `M * N - O`: how is M related to O?
3. `P / Q * R`: how is P related to R?
4. Pointing at a woman, Rohan says, "She is the daughter of my father's only son." Rohan has no brothers. Who is she to Rohan?
5. "Sudha's father is my father's son, and I have no brothers or sisters." How is the speaker related to Sudha?
6. `X + Y / Z`: how is X related to Z?
7. K is the son of L. L is the sister of M. M is married to N. How is K related to N?

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a paternal uncle and a maternal uncle?
flashcards.back: A paternal uncle is your father's brother; a maternal uncle is your mother's brother. 'Paternal' means the father's side, 'maternal' the mother's side.
flashcards.explanation: Questions that name the side expect you to use it.

flashcards.front: Two ways someone can be your brother-in-law?
flashcards.back: Your spouse's brother, or your sister's husband. Both are brothers-in-law by marriage, not by blood.
flashcards.explanation: In-law relations always pass through a marriage link.

flashcards.front: What symbols keep a family diagram unambiguous?
flashcards.back: Triangle for male, circle for female, box for unknown sex; a double line for marriage; a vertical line down to children, with one generation per horizontal level.
flashcards.explanation: A fixed notation stops the picture from drifting as facts pile up.

flashcards.front: Which way do you unpack a pointing-to-a-photo statement?
flashcards.back: From the far end back to the speaker: start at the last noun, move outward one link at a time, then swap 'my' and 'I' for the speaker.

flashcards.front: Why does the word 'only' matter in 'the only daughter of my grandfather'?
flashcards.back: It says the grandfather has exactly one daughter, which usually pins that person down to a single identity in the tree.
flashcards.explanation: Without 'only' the person could be any of several daughters.

flashcards.front: How do you evaluate a coded-relation expression such as 'P + Q - R'?
flashcards.back: Left to right, one symbol at a time, drawing each link into a diagram. Then read the asked relationship off the finished diagram.
flashcards.explanation: Each symbol is a fixed relationship; the diagram does the reasoning.

flashcards.front: Do you always need the sex of the end person to name a relationship?
flashcards.back: No. 'Grandparent', 'parent', 'child', 'sibling' and 'cousin' don't depend on sex, so answer at that level unless the question asks for more.
flashcards.explanation: Adding an unasked-for sex is a common way to mark a right answer wrong.
